content: 1. At post-treatment follow-up, significant improvement in self-reported social functioning was observed only in the SOF + RBV treatment group at post-treatment week 12. The reference regimen used for comparison was SOF + LDV. 2. Predictors of health-related quality of life impairment among adolescents with HCV included a history of asthma, mental disorders, abdominal pain, and sleep disorders, adjusted for age, sex, and location. These findings are consistent with previously reported data. 3. In the DORA 1 trial, which evaluated the safety and efficacy of GLC + PIB, quality of life was assessed using the PedsQL scale, a validated patient-reported outcome instrument for children with chronic health conditions. An increase in the PedsQL score from baseline indicates an improvement in quality of life. Among 44 adolescents treated with GLC + PIB, improvements were observed in the total PedsQL score, physical health summary score, and psychosocial health summary score. 4. Treatment of HCV infection with direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens was not associated with a decline in quality of life during therapy. Instead, improvements in health-related quality of life scores were noted after achieving sustained virologic response (SVR). 5. Among children aged 3–5 years, the strength of evidence for SVR12 was moderate for SOF + LDV (two studies, n=56). For all other DAA regimens evaluated in at least one study, the strength of evidence for SVR12 was very low due to limited patient numbers and imprecision. 6. Among children aged 6–11 years, the strength of evidence for SVR12 was moderate for SOF + DCV (two studies, n=34), GLC + PIB (one study, n=56), and SOF + LDV (four studies, n=178). The strength of evidence was high for SOF + RBV (three studies, n=102). For other DAA regimens, the strength of evidence was very low due to serious risk of bias, inability to assess consistency, and imprecision. 7. Among adolescents aged 12–18 years, the strength of evidence for SVR12 was high for SOF + DCV (eight studies, n=138) and moderate for GLC + PIB (one study, n=48), SOF + DCV or LDV (two studies, n=60), and SOF + LDV (19 studies, n=1349). For other DAA regimens, the strength of evidence was low or very low due to serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. 8. The primary finding of this review is that treating children and adolescents (3–17 years of age) with chronic HCV infection using DAAs is highly effective and safe, with efficacy and safety comparable to those reported in adults. 9. The SVR12 rate was 95% (95% CI: 89–99%) for young children (3–5 years), 99% (95% CI: 97–100%) for children aged 6–11 years, and 99% (95% CI: 98–100%) for adolescents (12–18 years). 10. No significant differences in SVR12 rates were observed among adolescents across the regimens of interest (SOF + DCV, SOF + VEL, and GLC + PIB). Similar efficacies were observed for other treatment regimens. 11. In the SOF + VEL trial, five adolescents did not achieve SVR12: one due to virological failure after discontinuing treatment for pregnancy, and four for non-virological reasons (e.g., loss to follow-up, early treatment discontinuation). 12. Among children aged 6–11 years, no significant differences in SVR12 rates were observed across the regimens of interest. In the SOF + VEL trial, five children did not achieve SVR12, none due to virological failure. Reasons included adverse events and difficulties in taking oral medication. 13. The efficacy of SOF + VEL (83%) for children aged 3–5 years was lower than that observed for GLC + PIB (92%) and other regimens (e.g., SOF + RBV, SOF + LDV, EBR + GZR, OBV + PTV + ritonavir + DSV + RBV). 14. No patients treated with SOF + DCV were reported in the 3–5-year-old age group. A pharmacokinetic analysis suggested that a 30 mg daily dose of DCV would achieve effective and safe exposure in children weighing 14 to <35 kg, but clinical validation is needed. 15. Data from safety analyses suggest that DAA treatment is safe and well-tolerated among children and adolescents. The rate of adverse events was high (72% for children aged 3–5 years, 53% for those aged 6–11 years, and 50% for adolescents), but serious adverse events and treatment discontinuations were uncommon. 16. Headache, fatigue, and nausea were the most frequently reported adverse events, with no clear differences between treatment regimens or age cohorts. 17. HCV infection in children negatively impacts quality of life, psychosocial and cognitive functioning, and caregiver stress. Data suggest that DAA treatment can improve quality of life and reduce the stigma associated with HCV positivity. 18. A cost-effectiveness analysis indicated that treating adolescents with chronic HCV is cost-effective compared to deferring treatment until adulthood, particularly when using currently available pangenotypic regimens. 19. Limitations of this review include reliance on non-randomized controlled trials, missing data (e.g., comorbidities, HCV acquisition route, viral load), and the absence of placebo arms or treatment comparison groups. However, the findings of high SVR12 rates and optimal safety were consistent across study designs, settings, and age groups. 20. No data were available on the use of SOF + DCV among children aged 3–5 years. Further clinical validation of pharmacokinetic findings is required to guide treatment recommendations for this age group.
